message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.
</author>

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
## Verdict

The pilot is valuable and most of the cost arithmetic is correct. But three claims the recommendation depends on don't hold up against the study's own data:

1. **Flats did not keep pace with houses.** Participation was 66% in houses and 21% in flats.
2. **The projection uses a 64% participation rate that doesn't appear anywhere in the pilot.** The pilot's overall rate was 57%.
3. **Brookfield can take only about 60% of the projected tonnage until 2029.**

Correct any one of these and the "fully funded" conclusion becomes marginal or fails. Cabinet shouldn't approve on the current basis, although a corrected version could still be approvable.

## What's right

- **Table 1 is internally consistent.** 2,112/3,200 = 66%, 168/800 = 21%, 2,280/4,000 = 57%.
- **Table 2 is arithmetically correct.** 6 × £165,000 ÷ 7 = £141,400 a year, and the lines sum to £733,400.
- **The per-tonne saving and net cost follow from the stated inputs.** £112 − £38 = £74 a tonne, and the net cost of £490,400 matches.
- **Contamination below 2% and falling missed-collection reports** are genuinely good results.
- **The pilot's housing mix matches the district.** Flats make up 20% of the pilot and 20% of the district, so the pilot's results should scale straightforwardly once the right figures are used.

## 1. Flats did not perform like houses

Section 2 and your covering note say participation "held up" across housing types. Table 1 shows **66% in houses against 21% in flats**, roughly a third of the rate. This is the largest gap in the pilot.

The district has about 10,400 flats, and they must be served too. Low participation in flats is a common pattern, usually caused by communal bin stores, lack of space and transient residents. The pilot's evidence points towards a different approach for flats, such as communal food bins or targeted engagement, which may have its own costs. It does not support a uniform service.

## 2. The tonnage projection is overstated

Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate". The pilot measured **57%**. The arithmetic confirms that 64% was used: 52,000 × 0.64 × 1.9 kg × 52 weeks ≈ 3,290 tonnes.

| Basis | Tonnes a year | Disposal saving |
|---|---|---|
| As stated (64%, 1.9 kg) | 3,290 | £243,000 |
| Pilot overall (57%, 1.9 kg) | 2,930 | £217,000 |
| By housing type (houses 66% × 1.9 kg, flats 21% × 1.4 kg) | **2,870** | **£212,000** |

The housing-type split is the most accurate basis, and it reduces the saving by about £31,000.

Pilot participation may also flatter the long-term rate. Six months includes a novelty effect, and food waste varies with the seasons.

## 3. Treatment capacity is short until 2029

Brookfield offers up to **1,800 tonnes** a year. The corrected projection is about 2,870 tonnes, leaving **about 1,070 tonnes a year with nowhere costed to go** until Brookfield expands.

- **If the surplus goes to the plant 46 miles away,** its gate fee and haulage costs aren't in the study.
- **If the surplus is incinerated,** the saving falls to 1,800 × £74 = £133,000. Burning separately collected food waste would also undermine the purpose of the service.

Treatment is only partly local, so your covering note's statement that it is local needs qualifying.

## 4. "Fully funded" doesn't survive the corrections

| Scenario | Disposal saving | Net cost | Against £520k allocation |
|---|---|---|---|
| As stated | £243,000 | £490,000 | +£30,000 |
| Corrected tonnage, all to Brookfield | £212,000 | £521,000 | **−£1,000** |
| Corrected tonnage, surplus incinerated | £133,000 | £600,000 | **−£80,000** |

The final row is roughly the cost if the surplus can't be placed elsewhere. In addition:
- **The £520,000 is provisional.** Government has "indicated" funding will be provided; nothing is confirmed.
- **Even the stated case is tight.** It has only a £30,000 (6%) margin.

## 5. Cost lines that appear to be missing

Your covering note says every cost line is shown. Several usual ones aren't, and each needs costing or explaining:

- **Cover for absence and spare vehicles.** Twelve operatives and six vehicles leave no allowance for leave, sickness or breakdowns. An allowance of 10–15% is typical.
- **Supervision and management.**
- **The dedicated phone line and web page** described in section 6.
- **Liners after the first three months.** Is the continuing supply inside the £88,000?
- **Crew costs.** Does the £34,000 per operative include on-costs?
- **Vehicle funding.** About £990,000 is needed upfront in 2026–27. The study shows depreciation but not how the purchase is funded, or whether separate capital funding already covers it.

## 6. Timetable risks

- **Vehicle lead time.** Ordering in December for March delivery assumes about three months. Specialist collection vehicles often take considerably longer, so confirm in writing with the supplier before relying on it.
- **No slack in March.** Vehicle delivery, crew training and caddy delivery to 52,000 households all fall in March, before a 5 April start. A late vehicle delays the whole launch.
- **Statutory deadline.** Confirm the legal date. My understanding is that the requirement for weekly household food waste collection in England applied from 31 March 2026, with transitional arrangements for some councils. If Thornbury has no such arrangement, an April 2027 start would already be late. That would change the decision from whether to proceed to how fast, and Cabinet should know.

## Smaller points

- **The 81% satisfaction figure** comes from "surveyed pilot households". Report the response rate and whether non-participants were included. Satisfied users are more likely to reply.
- **The "All" row** gives 1.9 kg per participating household. The weighted figure is 1.86 kg. This is trivial, but use the housing-type figures in the projection anyway.

## What Cabinet needs before approving

1. **Projection by housing type** at the pilot's actual participation rates, with a sensitivity case for lower long-term participation.
2. **A costed plan for flats.**
3. **A costed solution for the roughly 1,000 tonnes over Brookfield's capacity** until 2029, either through the 46-mile plant or by negotiating with Brookfield.
4. **A full cost table** including cover, supervision, the contact line, ongoing liners and vehicle funding.
5. **Confirmation of the funding allocation and the statutory deadline**, plus a written lead time from the vehicle supplier.

With those in place, the service may well still be affordable, and if the deadline has passed it may have to proceed regardless. But the decision should rest on the corrected figures, not on "fully funded".
